conservation.condition_narrative: The painting is unlined, well-stretched, and appears unvarnished with a relatively matte surface. There are stretcher bar cracks at the sides and bottom, some of which were present as early as 1956. The painting has the artist’s original cardboard backing taped to the stretcher and is housed in a silver-gilt reproduction “clamshell” style frame.
conservation.report_notes: Information provided for *Access O'Keeffe* by Art Institute of Chicago in 2025.
conservation.technical_description: The painting is executed on a single piece of canvas primed with white attached to a four-member stretcher with no crossbars. Faint graphite lines around the edges of some forms suggest at least local underdrawing, but infrared imaging and/or stereomicroscopic examination would be needed to confirm its presence. The work is relatively thinly painted with the canvas texture visible throughout most of the composition. O'Keeffe varied her strokes for different areas of the work, often relying on stiff-bristle brushes and paint of a paste-like consistency to create directional strokes for various forms. In the white background, she employed a palette- or painter's-knife for areas of contrasting flatness.

cr_data.provenance: Georgia O’Keeffe (1887–1986), New York and New Mexico, then Abiquiú, NM, from 1949 [on loan to the Art Institute of Chicago from 1949; letter from O’Keeffe to Daniel Catton Rich, Dec. 29, 1955; copy in curatorial object file]; given through the Alfred Stieglitz Collection to the Art Institute of Chicago, 1955. (Source: Art Institute of Chicago, 2025)
